blocks.text: with foresight and good sense
Conditions for alternative corrective actions
Correction is a help. Correction is not punishment.
Correction describes an immediate consequence, brought about deliberately and with care, in response to an action that is worth changing.
Correction is an immediate consequence of the dog's behaviour that the dog can recognise.
Correction is the alternative action to be trained, to which the dog is to be conditioned.
Correction is the training of alternative scenarios which contain, in various variations, a repeating, recognisable, intended basic pattern.
Correction is the logical training of helpful alternatives in order to avert harm. Correction is not punishment.
Incorrect corrections to avoid
Avoid emotional correction.
Correction should not be imprecise in time or place.
Correction must never be inappropriate.
Correction must not take place without a temporal connection to the wrong action.
Correction is not punishment!
…success lies in calm
What to consider when ignoring
Ignoring means leaving actions unnoticed that are to be classified as unproblematic now and in the future.
Note: ignoring does not necessarily mean that actions will stop in the future.
Ignoring is suitable for situational, de-escalating use, without any claim to lasting effect.
Ignoring is suitable for demanding behaviour, but only if the dog is not thereby provoked into further wrong actions.
When ignoring is wrong
Avoid ignoring when an action would have to be actively corrected.
Avoid ignoring offensive actions that should no longer occur in the future.
Avoid ignoring actions that lead to problematic consequences.
Ignoring is not a general substitute for active training.
…as a basis for alternatives
Strategies for interruption
Interruptions serve acute work in the situation when unwanted actions occur.
The earlier the attempt to interrupt, the more effective the ending of the action.
Interruptions are often only preparation for alternative conditioning.
Use visual or acoustic influences to distract the dog from its intention.
Important: interruptions often do not have a lasting effect as long as the distracting stimulus is still present.
When should interrupting be avoided?
Avoid interruptions without subsequent corrective alternatives (risk of immediate resumption).
Avoid attempts to interrupt when it is foreseeable from the outset that they will remain ineffective (negative learning effect).
Avoid interruptions when the dog is currently showing desired actions.
Avoid rough or loud interruption actions; this could make it harder to lead the dog in similar situations.
…the better training
Paths to lasting success
Replace unwanted response patterns with intelligent alternative actions.
Ask for the alternative performance exactly at the start of the wrong action.
Choose exercises that suit your dog's character and level of training and that are highly reliable.
Ensure a high training repetition rate in order to achieve strong consolidation of the alternative action.
Train at a sufficient distance from the source of distraction so that the dog can learn without stress.
Critical errors in conditioning
Avoid unclear content or instructions without a sufficiently trained response pattern.
Avoid excited, loud or stressed reactions during training.
Avoid training when the wrong action is already in full swing (lack of receptiveness). In that case, take the dog out of the situation until it is responsive again.
Avoid training when the dog is overwhelmed by environmental conditions or when the distance to the stimulus is too small.
Avoid panicked reactions.
What research shows about correction methods
Several studies have compared how training methods affect the well-being of dogs.
A review (Ziv, 2017) evaluated the existing research on aversive methods. It found associations with more stress behaviour, fear and poorer well-being in the dogs.

A Portuguese study (Vieira de Castro et al., 2020) compared dogs from training schools using different methods. In dogs from schools using predominantly aversive methods, more stress signals and higher cortisol levels in saliva were found.

Many of these studies show associations rather than a single cause. However, the direction of the results is clear and corresponds to the approach of this course: build alternatives instead of punishing.
Stress additionally impairs the ability to learn. A correction that unsettles the dog therefore makes it harder to train the desired alternative.
Building an effective alternative action
The alternative action must be incompatible with the unwanted behaviour. A dog cannot sit and jump up at a person at the same time.
Train the alternative first without the trigger, then at a large distance from the trigger, and reduce the distance only in small steps.
Change only one factor at a time: distance, duration or distraction.
Reward the alternative clearly, so that it becomes more attractive to the dog than the original behaviour.
Clarify the cause of the behaviour. Fear, frustration, overexcitement and insecurity require different approaches. In the case of fear, distance from the trigger and building security come first.
Sudden changes in behaviour can have physical causes. In this case, first have a vet check whether pain or an illness is present.
Recognising triggers and acting early
Every wrong action has warning signs, for example fixating, stiffening of the body, changed breathing or a tense tail.
The earlier you recognise these warning signs, the more easily you will succeed in asking for the alternative action before the wrong action begins.
Exercise: for two weeks, keep a log with four entries: trigger, the dog's early signs, your reaction and the alternative used.
Record the entries under “My reflection” at the end of this page. Recurring patterns show you which trigger you should train on first.
In the case of aggression towards people or dogs, consult a professionally qualified trainer at an early stage.

Sources: Ziv G. (2017): The effects of using aversive training methods in dogs – A review. Journal of Veterinary Behavior 19, 50–60. Vieira de Castro A. C. et al. (2020): Does training method matter? Evidence for the negative impact of aversive-based methods on companion dog welfare. PLoS ONE 15 (12).
Correction is never punishment, but constructive help.
Correct corrections always offer empathetic alternatives.
Show your dog how it can be done differently and offer it alternatives it can trust.
